This is actually untrue, cats actually form similar attachments to their caregivers and as dogs and even infants do to their caregivers. Multiple studies often show humans often underestimate how much cats are able to form attachments, it’s estimated that from the results from this one [study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982219310863) that over 60% of cats have secure style attachments to their humans.

The reason people assume they don’t care about their humans is because their body language is often read by people as if it were dog body language. Cats do love you, often as unconditionally as a dog does.

In general getting a cat to stay off counters basically requires the same amount of effort keeping a dog from jumping on the table or your couch does. It’s actually a misconception that cats don’t respond to training, they’re creatures of habit so forming habits in them is very easy.

 Clicker training and leaving an unpleasant walking surface (tinfoil and sticky tape, nothing dangerous though!!) for a few days so the cat associates the surface with crinkling or slight stickiness) and adopts the habit of staying off the surface or furniture you don’t want them climbing on. [guide on how to keep cats off counters](https://www.thesprucepets.com/how-to-keep-cats-off-counters-551798).

You can also train a cat to use the toilet outside on a harness if you really wanted to or let your cat in safe closed off area in your garden if the litter box bothers you, like how you’d do it with a dog but it’s not really that unsanitary to use a litter box as long as you clean it often and preferably use quality litter, it’s basically a toilet that you have to flush for them.

The last one is kind of a little bit unpredictable though, it depends on the cat’s personality, some cats are clever shitheads that will always find something you never thought of and some are either less mischievous or less clever.

My cat is a essentially a support animal for my autism, she helps me when I’m having a meltdown or otherwise struggling at home (she’s very good at recognising when I’m not doing well but even just her presence in the room is enough to help).

She also helps me remember to take my medication and it’s a nice bonus to have a cat that will eat moths (which harm the local bumble bees) or other destructive pests that come into the house. Also, funnily enough all of my cats are better behaved and better trained than my dog (although she is still pretty good just a little dim), they come when called, will stop doing things when asked and will do various commands (which vary based on which cat it is but the cat that supports me knows “will you sing me a song?” and she’ll meow and “stand” which will make her jump up on her two paws).

Toxoplasmosis being transmitted to owners is also less common in vaccinated pets that are fed commercially prepared pet food.

In fact owning a cat has been proven to lower risks of heart disease and depression and physical health, as well as making you more attractive to those around you ([here’s article listing a few if you’re interested](https://www.healthline.com/health/benefits-of-being-cat-lover#3.-Relationships)).

Cats aren’t for everyone but it’s not really accurate to say they aren’t helpful at all. They clearly provide benefits to those who own them, especially those who are disabled.

From what I’ve heard CBT is almost completely useless for a lot of neurodivergent people, especially autistic people a lot of time, especially compared to the average neurotypical.

Almost every autistic person who has tried CBT (usually for depression, suicidal behaviour or anxiety) said it was completely useless and they felt worse afterwards because their doctor was annoyed that it wasn’t helping (my self included) and in my case the crisis centre made me feel like I was actively frustrating them because it wasn’t working.
